hero.title: Work across organisations.
hero.intro: When an AI agent acts for a supplier, partner or public institution, your organisation needs to check its identity and permissions. Genesis Mesh helps separate systems answer three questions:
questions: What are you allowed to do?
hero.statement: Genesis Mesh helps organisations check digital proof and manage access across boundaries.
hero.body: Each organisation decides whose proof to accept, what actions to allow and when to withdraw permission. A sovereign is simply a separately controlled organisation or system. Its root of trust is the digital foundation it controls to issue and check proof.
hero.notLine: Each organisation keeps its own authority. No single authority controls everyone. No particular cloud is required.
hero.closing: Cooperate with partners. Keep your own rules.

trustCycle.label: A practical example
trustCycle.title: A supplier’s agent loses access when its proof is withdrawn.
trustCycle.subtitle: Illustrative scenario: a supplier’s AI agent asks to check a delivery status in your system. Your organisation recognises the supplier’s signed proof, but sets its own access rules. The technical demonstration below tests this accept-then-reject pattern; it is not a customer deployment.
trustCycle.sameRequest: Same agent. Same request. Permission is no longer valid.
trustCycle.after: After the withdrawal update is received

steps.title: The supplier identifies its agent
steps.description: The supplier issues signed digital proof for the agent. This is called an attestation.

steps.title: Your organisation recognises the supplier
steps.description: Your system records which proof it will accept from the supplier and for what purpose. Genesis Mesh calls this a recognition treaty.

steps.title: Your system allows the request
steps.description: The proof is valid and the request meets your access rules. Recognising the supplier does not give its agent unlimited access.

steps.title: The supplier withdraws the proof
steps.description: The supplier marks this agent’s proof as no longer valid. This is called revocation.

steps.title: Your system receives the update
steps.description: Your system checks the supplier’s signed withdrawal notice and updates its records. This step must happen before the withdrawal can affect this decision.

steps.title: The same request is denied
steps.description: The agent tries again. Your system rejects the request and records why, so the decision can be reviewed.

stakes.label: Your control
stakes.title: Work together without handing over control.
stakes.subtitle: Your organisation can recognise a partner’s digital proof while keeping its own access rules, infrastructure and authority.
stakes.notLine: Genesis Mesh handles the checks: who issued the proof, what it permits, whether it has been withdrawn and what evidence supports the decision.
stakes.boundary: People still decide policy, approve relationships and resolve disputes. The software does not create a legal agreement or settle a disagreement for you.

powers.label: Where it could help
powers.title: Different partnerships. Different access rules.
powers.subtitle: These are illustrative uses of Genesis Mesh. Recognising a partner’s digital proof does not mean accepting all of its policies or endorsing its activities.

close.title: Work regularly with a supplier.
close.desc: For example, a supplier’s agent could check delivery information under agreed access rules. Both organisations keep control of their own identities and permissions.
examples: Agree what each agent may do
Withdraw your own permissions when needed

scoped.title: Allow a specific job for a limited time.
scoped.desc: For example, a partner’s service could be recognised for one purpose during a project window. Your system still checks whether each request is allowed.

different.title: Cooperate without agreeing on everything.
different.desc: Two institutions could recognise specific digital proofs while keeping different internal policies. Recognition applies to the defined relationship.
examples: Either party can withdraw its own trust

mechanics.label: How it works
mechanics.title: Four checks your business can understand.
mechanics.subtitle: Genesis Mesh provides the technical checks. Your organisation decides the rules: which partners to recognise, what access to allow and when to stop it.

ops.name: Verify identity
ops.desc: Check who issued the digital proof and whether it is authentic. Digital signatures, including Ed25519, let systems detect altered or forged proof.

ops.name: Limit access
ops.desc: Define which actions are allowed and for how long. Recognising an agent does not give it permission to do everything.

ops.name: Withdraw permission
ops.desc: Publish a signed notice when proof is no longer valid. Other systems check and apply the update; withdrawal is not automatically instant everywhere.

ops.name: Review the evidence
ops.desc: Keep records of decisions that reveal later tampering. Your team can examine why a request was accepted or rejected.

evidence.title: Each organisation keeps its own trust foundation.
A withdrawal can be applied by another organisation.
Selected protocol properties are modelled in Tamarin, a security analysis tool.

protocol.label: Technical foundation
protocol.title: Open specifications your team can inspect.
protocol.subtitle: The main software and the TypeScript, Go, .NET and Rust developer libraries are coordinated at v{version}. The core test suite contains {tests} tests. Tamarin security models examine selected protocol properties; these are not a guarantee that every deployment is secure.

l1.name: Core checks
l1.desc: Check signed identities using Ed25519, enrol participants, withdraw proof, route messages and record evidence.

l2.name: Your organisation’s domain
l2.desc: Your separately controlled environment. You decide who joins, which rules apply and what to revoke.

l3.name: Relationships with other domains
l3.desc: Signed recognition agreements connect separately controlled systems and let them share withdrawal updates.

governance.label: How changes are decided
governance.title: Public proposals. Defined reviews.
governance.description: Changes to the technical rules are published for review. Maintainers review them, operators review changes to their obligations, and security reviews cover changes to trust decisions.
governance.boundary: The protocol is the set of rules; the reference implementation is software that follows them. Each operator keeps its own keys, policies, trust decisions and right to leave.

closing.title: Explore Genesis Mesh.
closing.subtitle: Choose a partner interaction. Define who needs access, what they may do and how that access should end. Then ask your team to test the flow.

operators.title: Keep control of your environment.
operators.desc: Set up your organisation’s authority, manage its signing keys, choose which partners to recognise and publish withdrawals when needed.

builders.title: Connect a test system.
builders.desc: Use the technical specifications and Python, TypeScript, Go, .NET or Rust tools to test on your own infrastructure. Check integration needs before planning a rollout.

strategic.title: Evaluate a concrete use case.
strategic.desc: Review the evidence with your security and technology teams. Discuss who sets the rules, who operates each authority and what happens when access is withdrawn.
